questions.q: What are the two essential components that define an angle when you are drawing it on paper?
questions.a: An angle is defined by a common starting point (the vertex) and two rays (the arms). A wrong answer (like saying "two lines") suggests the student confuses a line segment intersection with a formal angle construction.

questions.q: If you align your protractor and see your ray passing through both 0° and 180°, which scale should you look at to mark an angle of 40°?
questions.a: You must look at the scale that begins at 0° on the ray you are using. A wrong answer shows the student does not understand that the protractor has two scales for different ray orientations and is just picking a random number.

questions.q: You are asked to draw a 70° angle. After drawing your first ray and placing the protractor, you mark the point at 70°. If you connect the vertex to this mark, what is the most important thing to check to ensure your construction is correct?
questions.a: Check that the angle is acute (less than 90°) by looking at it—it should look "sharper" than a corner of a page. If the student draws an obtuse angle, it means they used the wrong scale on the protractor.

questions.q: Why is it incorrect to place the edge of the protractor on the ray instead of the centre mark (the origin) when measuring or drawing an angle?
questions.a: The centre mark is the vertex of the protractor's scale; if you use the edge, your starting point for the turn is shifted, leading to an inaccurate measurement. This reveals if the student understands the geometric "origin" of an angle.

questions.q: If a student marks 110° on the inner scale but uses the outer scale to read the position, why will the resulting angle be incorrect?
questions.a: The scales on a protractor are complementary (they add up to 180°). Reading the wrong scale results in an angle of 70° (180-110) instead of 110°, proving the student is not paying attention to which "0" mark the ray is touching.

questions.q: Design a quick "check" to tell if your classmate's 130° angle is likely correct without using a protractor.
questions.a: A good answer mentions that 130° is obtuse, so it must be wider than a square corner (90°) but narrower than a straight line (180°). A poor answer suggests "it looks big," which is too vague and lacks geometric reasoning.
